chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Drummer Randy Carroll and the Roy Eldridge lesson about lifting the out chorus
summary: Carroll learned the arrangements and plays flexible fills like Art Blakey; Horace taught Roy Eldridge to build to the out chorus the same way.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: And I've got an excellent little drummer with me, named Randy Carroll, and, thank God, he doesn't play loud, extra loud. He can. On of his solos -- he has a few things that he does by himself; (unintelligible) sometimes, and he keeps steady time. He's got real flexible wrists like the great Art Blakely, who was in Fletcher's band for a long time and I had the pleasure of being part of that rhythm section,

and he likes it a lot, and he plays real good. And he uses his brushes on things like that. When he first came into the group, he respected my judgment. He said, "How do you want me to do this, (Unintelligible) do a solo, so we did get a few things together. And we stopped and we talked, and I said, "I'd like this," you know, so and so. And he's got an uncanny memory. He sticks with that. And the thing about it, he has made it his business to learn the arrangements real thorough, and he makes the movements that a drummer should make. Rhythmmwise.
Catching and filling up the cracks, (Unintelligible) relax in the part,
you know, and he doesn't overdo it. He's just -- he glides, you know, and I like this.

And, you know, when you're playing a solo, if you're playing soft, he'll stay under you, which is good. And then at the end of your solo when you get ready to come in with your outchorus, he makes that fill in that --

-- brings you right in, which lifts the arrangements, you know. This is the thing I liked about Roy Eldridge, you know, when he was playing trumpet, and Roy said I was responsible for him learning how to do this, but I always told Roy, at the end of he can't do his solo, just build the thing up, so when they brought the band back in, you would give it that boost, and, tells (unintelligible) everybody.

And the same thing usually, if you'll notice, in Roy's earlier records I'd always tell him to -- when he'd get ready to play a chorus, if it didn't interfere with the man playing in front of him, or if it was an ensemble and then his chorus was next, to get him a start coming in, and he'd always do that, you know. He'd bring himself into this chorus before the first bar, and then he'd be in there. He says, 'Man, this gives me a lift. This gives me, This thing, you see. He never forgot that, and he gave me credit for telling him this.
